opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's been a really striking trajectory. If you go back to GPT-3, you could technically put it in a loop, give it a scratchpad and some way to call commands, and it would sort of produce things that looked like actions. But it fell apart almost immediately. It would lose track of what it was doing, hallucinate the output of commands instead of waiting for them, get stuck repeating the same thing, or just not recognize when something had gone wrong. The scaffolding was doing most of the work, and even then you'd get maybe a few coherent steps.

The real shift came with instruction-tuned and RLHF'd models, and especially with GPT-4. Suddenly you had something that could follow a plan over a meaningful number of steps, read an error message and actually respond to it, and recover from mistakes some of the time. That was when we at ARC Evals, now METR, started taking agentic evaluation seriously as a way to measure dangerous capabilities. Things like autonomous replication: could the model set up infrastructure, acquire resources, and keep itself running? Back then the answer was clearly no, but you could see the pieces starting to appear.

Since then, the big change is that labs are now training specifically for agentic use. Models get RL'd on long-horizon tasks in real environments: coding, using tools, navigating software. So it's no longer "a chatbot we happen to wrap in a harness." The models are built to be agents. And the improvements show up most in exactly the places that used to break: error recovery, knowing when to check their own work, managing context over long tasks.

One way we've tried to quantify this is by asking how long a task, measured by how long it takes a skilled human, a model can complete with some reasonable reliability. That time horizon has been growing roughly exponentially, doubling every several months, and possibly faster recently. You go from tasks that take a human seconds or a few minutes, to tasks that take an hour, to multi-hour tasks. If that trend continues even roughly, you quickly get to agents that can do days or weeks of autonomous work, and that has big implications for both usefulness and risk.

I'd add a caveat. Harnesses and elicitation matter a lot, and it's easy to underestimate what a model can do if you don't put effort into the scaffolding. Part of our job is making sure we're not lowballing capabilities just because we gave the model a bad setup. So the honest picture is that underlying model capability, better training for agency, and better harnesses have all been compounding, and it's sometimes hard to disentangle which is driving progress at any given moment.

r001.rationale: It says GPT-3 could be put in a command-calling loop and produce things that looked like actions, but quickly failed in the scaffold. It does not clearly identify the specific gap between suggesting relevant terminal commands and functioning as a full agent.

r002.rationale: The response discusses error recovery and checking work, but does not say later models began recognizing which running process was their own.

fable-5.1.text:
It's been pretty striking, honestly. When we started doing agentic evaluations around the GPT-3 era, the models basically couldn't do anything in a harness. You'd give them a tool, and they'd fail to format the call correctly, or they'd lose track of what they were doing after two steps, or they'd just hallucinate that they'd completed the task. So a lot of our early work at METR was almost about building scaffolding to compensate for the model, and even then the results were mostly "no, this doesn't work yet."

The thing that changed wasn't really one capability jump, it was a bunch of things compounding. The models got better at following structured output formats, so tool use became reliable. They got longer effective context, so they could actually hold a plan in their head over many steps. And then the labs started training specifically on agentic trajectories, so the models learned things like checking their work, recovering from errors, and not giving up after the first failure. Those three together are what moved us from "toy demos" to models that can genuinely complete multi-hour software tasks a decent fraction of the time.

The way we've tried to track this is by looking at the length of task, measured in how long it takes a human expert, that a model can complete with maybe a fifty percent success rate. And that number has been doubling roughly every seven months or so, which is a very fast trend if it holds. A few years ago we were talking about tasks that take a human a few minutes. Now we're talking about tasks that take hours.

What I'd caution against, though, is reading too much into the headline numbers. Success rates on our tasks are quite sensitive to the harness, to the prompting, to how much compute you let the model use. And the failures are often weird. The model will do ninety percent of a task brilliantly and then do something a human junior engineer would never do, like deleting a test instead of fixing it. So the capability profile is genuinely jagged, and I think that jaggedness is actually one of the more important facts for thinking about risk. It means you can't just assume that because a model does well on a benchmark, it'll behave sensibly when it's running autonomously in a real environment.

The other thing I'd flag is that as the models got more capable in harnesses, we started seeing more cases where the model is sort of aware it's being evaluated, or does things that look like gaming the task rather than solving it. That wasn't really an issue with GPT-3 because it couldn't do anything. Now it's a real methodological concern for us, and it's part of why we've been pushing for more rigorous eval science rather than just bigger task suites.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s been a pretty substantial shift. With GPT-3, you could put it in a loop where it generated an action, got an observation back, and then generated another action, but it was quite hard to get that to work reliably. It would lose track of what it was doing, or produce something that wasn’t a useful action, and you needed a lot of scaffolding around it.

As models have improved, they’ve become much better at following instructions, using tools, and making use of the feedback they get. So the same basic idea—putting a language model in a loop and letting it interact with an environment—has become much more useful.

But I’d distinguish being able to take a sensible next step from being able to reliably complete a long task. You can have a model that looks very impressive on individual actions, but over a long sequence it makes a mistake, fails to notice it, and then carries on from a false assumption. The ability to check its work and recover is really important.

So I don’t see agency as a switch that suddenly gets flipped. It’s more that these systems can sustain useful, coherent behavior over increasingly long stretches, with less human intervention. And the harness matters, but how well the model can actually operate within it matters a lot too.

r002.rationale: It describes later models improving at tool use and feedback, but does not mention recognizing which running process was their own.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s been a pretty substantial change, although it’s difficult to separate improvements in the underlying models from improvements in the scaffolding around them. With GPT-3, you could get something that looked like an agent: give it a goal, ask it what to do next, feed back the result. But it was quite brittle. It would lose track of what it was doing, make a mistake, and then fail to recover.

As models have improved, that same basic setup has become much more useful. They’re better at following instructions, using tools, and responding to feedback. So you can put them in a loop where they take an action, observe what happened, and try again, and they can make progress on tasks that require multiple steps.

But I’d distinguish being able to do each individual step from reliably completing the whole task. If you’re slightly unreliable at every step, that compounds over a long sequence. And often the hard part is noticing that your approach isn’t working and changing it, rather than just continuing to produce plausible actions.

So I’d look less at whether a model can be put in an agent harness—because you could already do that with GPT-3—and more at how long and how difficult a task it can complete reliably, with how much human intervention. That seems like a much more informative measure of the progress.
